item.title: Chad : Humanitarian Situation in Lac Situation Report N° 02 (30 October 2026)
item.description:
Country: Chad
Sources: CCCM Cluster, Education Cluster, Food Security Cluster, Government of Chad, Health Cluster, International Organization for Migration, Nutrition Cluster, Protection Cluster, Shelter Cluster, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, WASH Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

This report was produced by OCHA in collaboration with the authorities and humanitarian partners. It primarily covers the period from 1 to 30 October 2026 and incorporates findings from the July 2026 mid-term evaluation of the response to internally displaced persons (IDPs). The next report will be published at the end of November 2026.

KEY POINTS

  • 307,206 displaced people in the province according to IOM Round 26, including 268,064 IDPs, 17,100 returnees, and 22,042 former IDPs who have returned.
  • More than 75,000 IDPs have been hosted across 16 sites in the Fouli and Kaya departments since May 2026. New population movements continue to be reported and remain under verification.
  • An encouraging improvement in the cholera situation was observed between 13 and 26 October, followed by a resurgence of 12 new cases in Kiskawa. However, the case fatality rate remains high (5.78%), well above the WHO emergency threshold, requiring the need to strengthen prevention, surveillance, and WASH interventions.
  • The areas of Liwa, Kiskawa, Kadoulou, and Daboua are among those most exposed to security risks. This insecurity directly contributes to population displacement, loss of livelihoods, and reduced access to basic services.
  • Four incidents were reported in the departments of Fouli and Kaya, affecting several civilians and resulting in dozens of deaths as well as abductions, a toll that would have been even higher without the intervention of the defense and security forces.
  • Despite the scale of needs, the protection sector remains the least covered, with only 0.3% of targeted people assisted.
  • A concerning deterioration in livelihoods has been observed linked to low rainfall.
  • US$10.6 million has been mobilized through humanitarian emergency funding mechanisms, including CERF, the Regional Humanitarian Fund, and anticipatory action, to support the response.
  • Significant humanitarian needs remain unmet due to insufficient funding, particularly in protection, shelter and site management, education, health and nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
  • The revitalization of the Grand Cadre Nexus and the review of convergence zones offer an opportunity to strengthen integrated investments by linking emergency response, access to essential services, social cohesion, and resilience.

item.title: UNHAS South Sudan - Concept of Operations
item.description:
Country: South Sudan
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Aviation a critical enabler of humanitarian response in South Sudan, particularly for remote and hard-to-reach communities. In this context, UNHAS South Sudan serves approximately 48 destinations, transports more than 4,000 passengers each month, and supports around 200 humanitarian organizations through a fleet of 10 aircraft.

More than 50 percent of destinations are accessible only byhelicopter due to inadequate airstrip infrastructure and challenging operating conditions, particularly during the rainy season. While this creates significant cost pressures, the service maintains operational efficiency through optimized routing, multi-stop scheduling, flexible fleet deployment, and a cost-recovery mechanism, while retaining the capacity to respond to emergencies.

The overall service is governed by the Steering Committee and User Group Committee, ensuring that operational decisions and resources remain responsive to the evolving needs of the humanitarian community.

Beyond service delivery, UNHAS strengthens the safety and longer-term sustainability of humanitarian aviation in the country through rigorous aviation safety and security standards, stakeholder coordination, capacity building, and infrastructure development.

item.title: DR Congo: Cluster Protection RDC : Aperçu des violations et abus des droits humains dans la province du Nord-Kivu, octobre 2026
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: Protection Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

En octobre 2026, la situation de protection au Nord-Kivu est restée critique, marquée par une intensification des affrontements dans les territoires de Masisi, Walikale et Rutshuru. Cette situation se serait traduite par l’usage d’armes lourdes et de frappes de drone, des représailles contre les civils ainsi que des déplacements forcés.

FAITS SAILLANTS DE LA PÉRIODE

●Intensification des hostilités : Des affrontements auraient opposé un groupe armé à une coalition de groupes armés dans les territoires de Masisi et de Walikale, et des frappes de drone auraient visé Binza (Rutshuru).

●Déplacements forcés : Près de 2 580 ménages (environ 12 900 personnes) auraient été déplacés, dont 546 à Busanza (Rutshuru) et 450 à Kasake (Masisi).

●Engins explosifs : Des projectiles tombés sur Kasake auraient fait 4 morts et 6 blessés, et des engins explosifs largués sur Kangati auraient tué 2 garçons.

●Représailles et riposte Ebola : Des enlèvements contre rançon accompagnés de meurtres et des attaques de structures sanitaires à Butembo et Beni auraient été commis.

item.title: Lebanon: Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) - Midyear Report 2026
item.description:
Country: Lebanon
Sources: UN High Commissioner for Refugees, United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

The Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) Midyear Report 2026 presents an analysis of GBV incidents reported to 18 participating service providers across Lebanon between January and June 2026, comparing findings with the same period in 2025. The report examines trends in reported incidents, survivor profiles, displacement-related risks, access to services, and referral gaps against the backdrop of renewed hostilities, widespread displacement, and increasing humanitarian needs.

The report identifies a 32% decrease in reported GBV incidents compared with the first half of 2025. However, this decline should not be interpreted as a reduction in GBV prevalence. Conflict-related disruptions, reduced availability of services, funding constraints, displacement, and barriers to safe disclosure have affected survivors' ability to access assistance and report incidents.

Key findings include:

  • Women and girls accounted for 99% of reported survivors, while adults represented 92% of survivors.
  • Intimate partner violence (IPV) remained the predominant case context, accounting for 90% of reported incidents, with a 9% increase in reported IPV cases compared with midyear 2025.
  • Psychological/emotional abuse (39%) and physical assault (38%) were the most frequently reported forms of GBV.
  • Internally displaced persons accounted for 20% of reported survivors, highlighting the impact of renewed hostilities and displacement on protection risks and access to services.
  • Nearly one-third of survivors (29%) sought assistance more than one month after the incident, reflecting persistent barriers to timely reporting and support.
  • Significant service gaps remain, including limited access to specialized mental health services, with 52% of mental health referrals reported as unavailable, alongside gaps in livelihoods and recovery support.

The findings highlight how conflict, displacement, economic hardship, and reductions in humanitarian funding continue to affect GBV risks and survivors' access to essential services. The report calls for strengthened GBV risk mitigation in displacement settings, sustained survivor-centred case management and referral services, improved access to specialized mental health and economic recovery support, and greater investment in preventing and responding to intimate partner violence.

The report aims to inform evidence-based humanitarian programming, coordination, advocacy, and resource allocation to ensure continued access to safe, confidential, and quality GBV services across Lebanon.

Data limitation: GBVIMS findings reflect incidents reported by survivors who accessed participating service providers and consented to the anonymized use of their information. They do not represent the total number of GBV incidents or measure GBV prevalence in Lebanon.

item.title: World: ICRC: Explosive remnants of war continue to kill and maim civilians long after the fighting ends
item.description:
Country: World
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Statement on the occasion of 20th Annual Conference of the High-Contracting Parties to Protocol V of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, 12 November 202

In many parts of the world, explosive remnants of war litter cities, agricultural fields and countrysides that are no longer battlefields. They continue to kill and maim thousands of civilians every year despite active hostilities having ended long ago. According to the Landmine and Cluster Munitions Monitor, in 2025, a large proportion of victims of mines, cluster munitions and explosive remnants of war were children.

In our work in armed conflicts around the world, we witness every day how explosive remnants of war impede access to health-care facilities and other essential services. They block transport and escape routes, hinder the delivery of life-saving humanitarian assistance and hamper agriculture and trade. In post-conflict settings, explosive remnants of war delay reconstruction efforts and prevent the return of displaced people to their home areas. In 2024, according to the Landmine Monitor, 52 states and territories remained affected by anti-personnel mines and other explosive remnants of war. This indicates the magnitude of the issue.

Mr. President,

The use of heavy explosive weapons in populated areas multiplies the human cost of conflict, including by leaving behind explosive remnants of war that continue to endanger civilians long after the fighting has ended. Historic and recent conflicts are clear examples.

The ICRC and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement call on all states and parties to armed conflict to avoid the use of explosive weapons with a wide impact area in populated areas. This means that these weapons should not be used in populated areas unless sufficient mitigation measures can be taken to reduce the weapons’ wide-area effects and the consequent risk of civilian harm. The landmark Political Declaration on Strengthening the Protection of Civilians from the Humanitarian Consequences Arising from the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas, which, to date, has been endorsed by 91 states, marks significant progress in this respect. We encourage all states to endorse the Declaration and to implement it effectively. Furthermore, and given the significant presence of civilians in urban areas, we urge states to make particular efforts to ensure full compliance with their obligations under Protocol V when using explosive weapons in cities or other populated areas.

Mr. President,

Approximately half the world's states are party to Protocol V. The rate of its universalization has slowed down but not stalled completely. We would like to congratulate Serbia, which has consented to be bound by Protocol V and look forward to their becoming the 100th state party to the Protocol in March 2027. We urge all states that are not yet party to Protocol V to adhere to it and we remind all States Parties to remain steadfast in implementing their obligations under it.

In the past year, the ICRC has promoted Protocol V to states bilaterally and at regional forums in South Asia, South-East Asia and the Caribbean.

Mr. President,

Today, the ICRC partners with 20 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, with more than 2,100 staff and volunteers, working alongside communities to help reduce their exposure to the risks posed by mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. This work includes technical support in clearance operations, raising awareness of and promoting safe behaviour, physical rehabilitation services, and support for the social and economic inclusion of survivors.

Our Advisory Service on IHL and colleagues in New York, Geneva and in ICRC delegations in capital cities around the world stand ready to continue assisting states in joining and implementing the Protocol.

item.title: UNICEF Zambia Humanitarian Flash Update No.1 (Cholera Outbreak), 16 November 2026
item.description:
Country: Zambia
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

  • Outbreak Overview: As of 16 November 2026, ZNPHI reported 3,099 cases and 68 deaths (CFR 2.2%) across 27 districts in seven provinces since 28 July. Children under 15 make up 24.9% of cases with age data (available for ~78.5% of cases).
  • Lusaka and Chibombo are the current hotspots accounting for 75.2% of cases (1,959 and 371 respectively).
  • Community engagement and communication: UNICEF-supported household visits reached over 1.2 million people, while dialogues engaged a further 30,000 people and 1,390 gatekeepers and influencers. This was reinforced by 31,600 communication materials (distribution underway) and a media campaign with an estimated potential audience of 7.8 million.
  • OCV: 701,354 vaccinations supported in Lusaka, Chibombo and Chongwe (23–26 October 2026).
  • WASH: UNICEF delivered 20 AWD kits to five districts and two tents to Chibombo for cholera treatment centres. It supported three inline chlorinators in Chibombo and WASH/IPC supplies to 20 health facilities in Chibombo and to treatment facilities in four Luapula districts.
  • Funding: UNICEF’s cholera response 2026/27 is only 9% funded, with a US$2.95 million gap (91%); Health has the largest gap (US$1.64 million). Urgent funding is needed to replenish WASH supplies and scale up treatment and community case finding before the rainy season.

item.title: World: Global Update | November 2026: An Inter-Agency Report of the Global ENSO Analysis Cell - El Niño Status & Humanitarian Outlook
item.description:
Countries: World, Afghanistan, Angola, Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cambodia, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Colombia, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Fiji, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Marshall Islands, Micronesia (Federated States of), Mozambique, Myanmar, Nepal, Nicaragua, Niger, Nigeria, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Philippines, Saint Lucia, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Somalia, South Sudan, Sri Lanka, Sudan, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania, Vanuatu, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of), Viet Nam, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Save the Children, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

OVERVIEW: WHAT HAS CHANGED SINCE SEPTEMBER

THIS MONTH

  • Forecast indicates further strengthening of El Niño. WMO now forecasts about +3.8°C for November–January, up from +3.6°C for September–November, with the positive Indian Ocean Dipole declining.
  • Risks flagged in September are materialising. South Sudan is having its driest year on record and Sudan faces famine risk in Darfur and Kordofan. The Dry Corridor’s IPC 3+ projection has doubled, 20 of 22 provinces in PNG are in extreme or severe drought, and FEWS NET warns that Famine (IPC Phase 5) could become the most likely outcome in southern Somalia if flooding becomes widespread and severe.
  • Anticipatory action has scaled up. OCHA-facilitated coordinated anticipatory action, funded by CERF and countrybased and regional pooled funds, is under way in 12 countries, with frameworks activated in seven and US$52.1 million allocated. CERF has provided a further US$11.5 million for early action in three countries, bringing OCHAmanaged pooled funding for El Niño to US$63.6 million; CERF’s own allocations have risen from US$28.4 million in September to US$52.5 million, supporting an estimated 2 million people. UN agencies, the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement and NGOs have also acted on their own or national triggers, often in the same countries: WFP alone has reached more than 1.3 million people in 17 countries, and FAO has acted in 15.
  • New appeals have been launched, by WHO (US$35.1 million) and IOM (US$110 million), alongside the FAO–WFP appeal and the Honduras Flash Appeal. In Sudan, the Humanitarian Country Team has set out a dedicated six-month El Niño operational response for 3.86 million people in Darfur and Kordofan (US$359.7 million, to March 2027). UNICEF has issued a global El Niño call to action covering 40 priority countries, which identifies a gap of about US$2.83 billion against its existing 2026 appeals, and an Asia-Pacific investment case of US$121.4 million.

item.title: Pakistan: Inter-Agency Winterization Strategy 2026 - 2027
item.description:
Country: Pakistan
Sources: International Organization for Migration, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

1. General

Pakistan experiences winter conditions primarily from November to February, with severe cold and snowfall concentrated in northern and high-altitude regions. Winter-related hazards include cold waves, heavy snowfall, avalanches, landslides, blizzards and fog, with varying impacts across the country. Mountainous areas face extreme temperatures and seasonal isolation, while communities in the plains may experience cold nights and damp conditions.

While Pakistan did not experience a major nationwide climate-related disaster in 2026 comparable to the previous year's floods, localized flooding affected parts of Gilgit-Baltistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Balochistan, resulting in localized damage to housing, infrastructure and livelihoods. An earthquake in the Upper Hunza area near the Wakhan Corridor further heightened concerns for affected mountain communities, where prolonged winters, sub-zero temperatures and seasonal access restrictions can significantly increase exposure risks. Households with damaged or inadequate shelters, particularly those in remote high-altitude settlements, may face heightened vulnerabilities during winter 2026–27. These localized impacts, together with residual vulnerabilities from previous disasters, reinforce the need for geographically targeted gender and age-responsive winterization assistance based on verified household needs and current shelter conditions.

According to NDMA's Disaster Early Warning–4 (DEW-4), October–December 2026, seasonal snow cover is projected to expand progressively across the Hindu Kush, Karakoram and western Himalayan ranges, beginning in October and becoming more extensive and persistent during November and December. The principal areas of concern include Gilgit-Baltistan, Upper Chitral, high-altitude districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and mountainous areas of Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Western Disturbances are expected to remain the primary drivers of significant snowfall episodes, while broader climate variability, including the El Niño– Southern Oscillation (ENSO), may influence seasonal weather patterns. Successive snowfall events, persistent freezing conditions and localized avalanche risks could disrupt road connectivity, restrict humanitarian access and isolate remote communities, particularly along high-altitude transport corridors.

These projections, together with seasonal advisories from PMD and consultations with PDMAs, GBDMA and SDMA, provide the basis for geographically differentiated winter-risk assessments and prioritization for 2026– 27.

item.title: Guidance Note and Standard Operating Procedure on the South Sudan Collective Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) Platform (Updated 3 August 2026)
item.description:
Country: South Sudan
Sources: Concern Worldwide, International Organization for Migration, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Purpose of the Collective AAP Platform

The South Sudan Collective AAP Platform will strengthen how AAP data (what communities are telling us and asking us to act on) is systematically brought into strategic and operational decisionmaking.

The Platform will consolidate existing de-identified AAP data from a range of sources into a format that allows us to identify trends, identify emerging issues, and inform programmatic adjustments at the inter-agency level, and ensure that decisions from leadership are influenced by community data. The responsibility for addressing individual complaints remains with individual organisations. The Platform should not duplicate efforts or be a parallel system to existing practices.

The intention is for the Platform to be a simple tool that is not an onerous additional stream of reporting for contributing organisations. It seeks to complement existing systems, enabling the trends in what communities are telling us to have a wider and more influential reach.

It provides aggregate information on trends, and is not designed, or intended, to single out individual organisations.

item.title: Syrian Arab Republic: Population Mobility and Baseline Assessment — Round 20 (01–30 September 2026)
item.description:
Countries: Syrian Arab Republic, Jordan, Lebanon, Türkiye
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

Since the transition of power on 8 December 2024, the Syrian Arab Republic (hereafter referred to as Syria) has experienced substantial shifts in its humanitarian, political, and demographic landscape. Population movements remain dynamic, with returns recorded across all 14 governorates alongside continued displacement. While changing security conditions have influenced mobility patterns, persistent gaps in housing, livelihoods, and access to essential services continue to affect the ability of returnees to re-establish their lives and sustain their return. The escalation of hostilities across the Middle East since 28 February 2026 has further influenced displacement dynamics, contributing to continued cross-border movements. This report presents mobility trends recorded during September 2026 by the International Organization Migration's (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), together with updated baseline estimates for Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), IDP returnees within Syria, and arrivals from abroad, including both those returning to their areas of origin and those settling elsewhere. This report should be read alongside Communities of Return Index Round 5 for additional context. The findings in this report provide an evidence base to support humanitarian response, early recovery programming and planning for durable solutions.

item.title: Yemen: Escalation in the Middle East and Beyond — Mobility Report (03 to 16 November 2026)
item.description:
Countries: Yemen, Afghanistan, Djibouti, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Türkiye
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

On 17 June 2026, the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran reached an agreement on a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) concerning the cessation of hostilities. The escalation in the Middle East and beyond had triggered a humanitarian crisis affecting multiple regions in an already fragile context. A resurgence of hostilities in recent weeks is placing pressure on humanitarian access and threatens civilian and essential services. Mobility dynamics across the region and beyond due to renewed escalation remains uncertain. The situation continues to be highly fragile, requiring sustained monitoring and operational preparedness.

In the Islamic Republic of Iran, the humanitarian situation continues to be shaped by recurring escalations. Disruption to basic services and infrastructure persist while restrictions on maritime and air transports have affected movement and humanitarian access. Overall, population movements remain localized, temporary, and economically driven, with no signs of mass displacement.

In Yemen, displacement increased significantly following the escalation of conflict along the West Coast in early September 2026. Between 07 June and 16 November 2026, IOM Yemen DTM recorded approximately 354,335 displaced individuals, the majority of whom were hosted in Ta’iz and Lahj governorates. Many families are experiencing repeated movements and seeking refuge in already overstretched displacement sites and host communities. In addition, as of 18 November, 4,336 Yemeni nationals arrived in Djibouti, reportedly fleeing the deteriorating security situation. In Lebanon, displacement nationwide remains significant despite continuing returns. As of 28 October 2026, 304,520 people remain internally displaced across 528 cadasters, a 8 per cent decrease compared to the previous reporting period (as of 29 September 2026). Returns have continued, with 964,689 returned IDPs reported as of 29 September 2026, marking a 10 per cent increase from the previous round (as of 29 September 2026).4 Meanwhile, cross-border flows into the Syrian Arab Republic are continuing, with a total of 1,021,966 movements recorded as of 16 November 2026. Sources include DTM Syria, in coordination with border authorities, the Iraq Border Point Commission, and Pakistani authorities. Increases and decreases noted are week to week changes

item.title: GIEWS Country Brief: Guatemala 19-November-2026
item.description:
Country: Guatemala
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

FOOD SECURITY SNAPSHOT

  1. El Niño curtails 2026 Primera maize harvest
  2. Postrera maize output anticipated below average, amid adverse weather and high production costs
  3. Cereal import requirements forecast above average in 2026/27
  4. El Niño‑related crop losses led prices of white maize and black beans up in September 2026
  5. About 2.6 million people projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity between October 2026 and February 2027

El Niño curtails 2026 Primera maize harvest

Harvesting of 2026 Primera maize crops concluded in October and production is preliminary estimated at 1.6 million tonnes, about 30 percent below average. Prolonged drought conditions between April and September 2026, associated to the onset of El Niño event, significantly affected crop development and caused substantial crop losses, particularly in the southern Dry Corridor, where most households depend on small‑scale rainfed agriculture for their livelihoods and food consumption. In key producing regions of Alta Verapaz, Izabal and western Petén, precipitation amounts in July and August 2026 were insufficient to offset the negative impact of moisture deficits at planting times, resulting in reduced yields. In addition, high fuel prices since March 2026, associated to the conflict in the Middle East and compounded by the termination of fuel subsidies in July increased production costs and further constrained maize production across the country.

Postrera maize output anticipated below average, amid adverse weather and high production costs

The 2026 minor Postrera maize crops, which account for about 35 percent of the annual production, are currently at development stage. Significant soil moisture deficits associated with El Niño phenomenon delayed land preparation and sowing operations, in some areas up to one month. Rain shortages and above‑average temperatures also discouraged planting intentions, particularly among subsistence farmers in the Dry Corridor. In September 2026, the government launched the Drought Emergency Response Action Plan, backed by an investment of USD 65 million, to mitigate the impact of severe drought conditions on agriculture and food security. Among its measures, the plan provides food assistance to more than 1.2 million households between September and December 2026.

Between mid‑September and October 2026, abundant rainfall amounts partially replenished soil moisture conditions, but localized torrential precipitations saturated soils and caused floods, river outflows and landslides, resulting in crop losses, particularly in key producing central‑eastern departments and southern Dry Corridor regions. Excessive moisture also increased incidence of pest infection across the country, further reducing yield prospects. Despite measures introduced in the last quarter of the year to contain increases of fuel prices, high production costs and an unfavourable weather outlook continued to constrain sowings. Looking ahead, El Niño‑related dry weather conditions are expected to intensify with the onset of the dry season in November 2026, further affecting crop development. As a result, the 2026 Postrera harvest is anticipated to be below average.

Cereal import requirements forecast above average in 2026/27

In the 2026/27 marketing year (July/June), cereal import requirements are forecast at an above‑average level, mainly driven by strong import demand for yellow maize by the feed industry and for white maize and wheat‑based food products for human consumption, in line with population growth. El Niño‑induced domestic production shortfalls have further increased import needs, prompting the government to nearly double the previously approved duty-free quota for white maize in July and in November, raising it to a record level of 175 million tonnes to be imported within December 2026.

El Niño‑related crop losses push white maize and black bean prices up in September 2026

Wholesale prices of white maize increased for four consecutive months between June and September 2026, reaching their highest level in four years. The sharp increase reflected significant losses to the Primera season harvest caused by drought conditions, which tightened domestic supplies, while rising fuel prices added upward pressure. In October, prices declined sharply by 16 percent, as markets were supplied by the late crop harvest from northern and central regions, and were about 7 percent higher compared to the previous year. Similarly, prices of black beans rose by 20 percent between September and October 2026, after remaining broadly stable from May to August. This is due to the tight market supply from the drought‑affected Primera season crops, harvested in September with a one‑month delay, as well as rising transport costs. Despite the recent increase, prices in October were only slightly above their year‑earlier levels. After several months of stability, rice prices increased seasonally in September and October 2026 and were moderately higher year‑on‑year, reflecting tighter market availability.

About 2.6 million people projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity between October 2026 and February 2027

According to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis, about 2.6 million people, approximately 14 percent of the analysed population, are projected to face acute levels of severe food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 [Crisis] or above) between October 2026 and February 2027, a level broadly unchanged from the September 2025 to January 2026 period. The highest concentration is expected in central Alta Verapaz, Huehuetenango and Quiche regions. Despite some seasonal improvements following the harvest, remittances inflows and improved seasonal income‑generating opportunities, rising food prices and depleted food stocks continue to constrain access to food among vulnerable households. In the Dry Corridor, food security conditions are expected to deteriorate markedly in the Ch’orti’ Region between November 2026 and March 2027, reflecting depleted food stocks and unfavourable production prospects for the Postrera harvest.
